chapter_theme: In the Ratanupura palace the princess hymns the god and brings his flower remnant to her father, who praises her in images of mango, moon and Ganga, then is troubled over whom to give her to and, after weighing love against the treatise, sends for the ministers learned in policy.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed in these verses
the Jain god the princess hymns
king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, her father

215.reading: The king's daughter hymns the god as the one who cut off desire and was wrathful at Death, the lord with the bright mark on his breast, whose flower-like feet she and her women bow to.
215.nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2 word for word in the edition; the repetition is kept as a text problem rather than a second statement.

claims.claim: the god has overcome desire and Death

216.reading: The hymn goes on: the god gave grace, ended deep sorrow, is the one lord of the wheel and of the world, and she bows at his feet to speak of his graceful words.
216.nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2 in the edition, as in the verse before.

claims.claim: the god's grace ends deep sorrow

217.reading: The spear-eyed girl, having praised the god in such words that keep off the fearsome enemy of deeds, wears the remnant of his holy feet's flowers.
217.event: The princess ends her hymn and puts on the flower remnant from the god's feet.

claims.claim: praise of the god keeps off the fearsome enemy of deeds

218.reading: Having taken the honey-rich flower remnant from the god's feet, the girl walks, praised by her doe-eyed companions, to the temple-like palace of her father's rich city.
218.event: The princess, praised by her companions, goes to her father's palace.

219.reading: Someone tells the king, goes gently up with feet that praise, and holds out the flower remnant in a red palm whose soft fingers turn red.
219.nuance: The final verb is masculine (நீட்டினான்) though the princess has been the actor in the two verses before; the sense of who offers the remnant, and the words ending line 2 and starting line 3, cannot be fixed.
219.event: The god's flower remnant is held out to the king in a palm.

220.reading: The king smells the crown of the hair of his daughter, who bows like a creeper while bees leave her lily-like flowers, and begins to say these things.
220.event: The king smells his daughter's hair-crown and begins to speak to her.

221.reading: The king tells her that though many bunches of nectar flowers stand, only the mango cluster makes spring appear, and he shines because she was born to him.
221.nuance: Her birth is praised as what lights the father and the house, a view of a daughter that the following four verses repeat in other images.

222.reading: The king says that where Ganga water flows even the sea becomes sacred, and that since her birth his family has been made known to the world and the seas' neighbours bowed.

223.reading: The king says that, as the base creatures do not touch a lotus pool, the whole region has fallen away from lowness since her birth.
223.nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe; the king's claim may be that lowly people stay clear of the realm because of her.

224.reading: The king says that as the young moon growing in the sky makes the world glad and dispels darkness, so her growth dispels the darkness in the house.

225.reading: The king says that as a bee comes in love to the jasmine and the lone champak grove, she is a fortune among women, whose house makes the whole earth glad.

226.reading: Having said such praise of her ornaments to the red-lipped girl, the king tells her to go into her mother's house and eat the meal.
226.event: The king bids his daughter go to her mother's house and eat.

227.reading: Telling her to wear anklets, not heavy ornaments, and walk gently, the golden king looks fondly on his daughter.
227.event: The king sends her off wearing anklets and watches her go.

228.reading: The king reflects that even if mortals seized every earthly jewel by force and won every heavenly one by fate, a girl as a jewel is hard to come by, a thing past counting.
228.nuance: The edition's word division makes the speaker's own judgement of her worth hard to separate from the narrator's report that he thought so (line 4).
228.event: The king ponders his daughter's worth beyond all treasure.

claims.claim: a daughter is a jewel beyond every treasure of earth and heaven

229.reading: The king asks which youth among the spear-bearing sons of the ancient mountain-kings is fitted by quality for her, which marked hero of the body and brave.
229.event: The king wonders who among the Vidyadhara youths is worthy of his daughter.

230.reading: The king reasons that though fine jewels may be set with soft flowers, and elders may join girls where families do not mingle, women with sad curls would not say no.
230.nuance: The sense of lines 3 and 4 turns on குலம் கலந்தில்வழி and on the sandhi of அன்றென்கிற்பவோ; the verse may mean that a daughter would not refuse an ill-matched union.

claims.claim: a match of unmingled families made by elders leaves the girl unable to refuse

231.reading: The king thinks that if parents give girls away with only the groom's side's gain in mind, girls whose hearts are not in it can only grieve and speak otherwise.
231.nuance: The word அந்தை (line 1) is rare and the grammar compressed; the reading of lines 1 and 2 is provisional.

claims.claim: parents who give a girl only for the groom's side's sake leave her grieving

232.reading: The king concludes that love is known only through love, outsiders cannot weigh a woman's desire by their own judgement, so in her matter he should follow the words of those who recite the treatise.
232.nuance: The verse gives two guides in tension: the girl's own love, which no outsider can judge, and the treatise's ruling, which the king chooses to follow; it does not say whether her love will be asked.

claims.claim: a girl's desire is known only by love, not by an outsider's reckoning
in a woman's marriage one should follow the way of those versed in the treatise

233.reading: The king reasons that a ruler's life is of two kinds, his own senses and those joined to others', and so ministers urge him to act on his own judgement.
233.nuance: The syntax of lines 1 and 2 is compressed, and whether the ministers urge the king or are urged by him cannot be fixed from the Tamil.

234.reading: The king reflects that though lotuses stand in cool pools they open by the sun's rays, and kings dwelling among virtue's groves likewise open by those who consider with learning.

claims.claim: a king flourishes only through learned poets and counsellors

235.reading: The king says that a boat on the great flower-sea reaches its shore if it sails true to the five times, and that those who enter with the learned's skill will find the sea of the elders' conduct.
235.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe in the edition's word division, including the 'five' of line 2.

claims.claim: going with the learned's depth lets one reach the limit of the elders' conduct

236.reading: The king notes that what one takes for good another finds not so, but one thing stands: the world accepts what accords with the treatise of policy.

claims.claim: the world accepts what accords with the treatise of policy

237.reading: The king says that brahmin conduct and kings' lives, without counsel, do not flower, and that even Indra's lordship is borne up by the thousand masters of the treatise.
237.nuance: The Indra and the thousand 'masters of the treatise' (ஈரைஞ்ஞாற்றுவர் தந்திரக் கிழவர்) are brought in as a Vedic and Brahmanical example in the king's own argument; the verse makes no Jain claim.

claims.claim: brahmin conduct and kings' lives need counsel to flourish
even Indra's rule is borne by masters of the treatise

238.reading: Having so reasoned in his mind, the king sends his men to summon the ministers who are masters of the treatise of policy, and they go to say what he has commanded.
238.event: The king sends messengers to bring his ministers learned in policy to counsel him on his daughter's marriage.

links.note: The king's question in verse 229, which youth is fit for his daughter, is met in verse 238 by sending for the ministers learned in policy.
links.teaches: The king does not choose the groom himself but turns his open question into a council of treatise-learned ministers, so the epic makes a marriage a matter for counsel.

links.note: The poet's opening hymn praises the god who conquered the sum of his deeds; the princess's hymn here names what he conquered, desire and Death.
links.teaches: The invocation praises the god's victory in general terms, while the princess's hymn names the enemies; one is left to see that the poem's single praise is told twice, in two voices.

links.note: Kural 445 tells a ruler to take counsel from ministers as his eyes; verse 237 says that kings' lives and even Indra's lordship do not flower without counsel.
links.teaches: The epic widens the Kural's rule from a ruler's prudence to a claim about all rule and even the gods' rule.

gains.a: A statement of the rule as a duty of a ruler, where the verse shows only that counsel is needed.
gains.b: An example from the Brahmanical and divine world that the couplet's own kings never reach.

links.note: Kural 445 calls counsellors a ruler's eyes; verse 234 pictures a king opening like a lotus by the sun only through the learned who consider.
links.teaches: The epic gives a picture of how counsel acts, a bloom that opens only at the sun's touch, where the Kural gives a rule that counsel should be taken.

gains.a: A plain rule that counsel is to be taken, behind its picture of the lotus.
gains.b: A figure that shows kingship as a bloom needing the light of the learned.

links.note: Naladiyar 274 uses a daughter of the house, enjoyed by a stranger, as a figure for wealth that others will use; verse 228 calls a girl the jewel beyond all earthly and heavenly jewels.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's picture treats a daughter's going to another house as a thing to be expected, while the epic makes her the treasure whose giving is a king's weightiest care.

gains.a: A plain statement that a daughter's passage to a stranger is as sure as hoarded wealth falling to another.
gains.b: A measure of how much the girl was worth to the one who gives her, which the simile treats as a mere example.

source_issues: Verses 215 and 216: line 3 repeats line 2 word for word in the edition (a doubled line).
Verse 219: the words ending line 2 and starting line 3 and the subject of the final verb cannot be resolved; flagged uncertain.
Verses 223, 230, 231, 233, 235: lines hard to construe in the edition's word division; flagged uncertain.
